title: KV tessellation allocator and fragmentation healing playbook
creator: Diego Morales
description:
Problem statement:

Our KV cache on GPU shows long-tail fragmentation patterns under mixed-length chat workloads with continuous batching enabled. Small lived entries (per-step activations, short completion tokens) interleave with long-lived conversational prefixes and pinned system tokens, producing unusable micro-holes that increase memory pressure and force early evictions of truly hot contexts. This increases re-computation, hurts p99 latency, and inflates token cost.

Goal:
Deliver a pragmatic allocation and healing strategy that: (1) reduces fragmentation amplification under continuous batching, (2) preserves low-p99 latency for hot contexts, (3) keeps implementation risk low and enables progressive rollout across Dedicated/Hosted runtimes.

High-level approach (tessellation allocator + healing):
- Introduce a tessellation allocation layer that subdivides GPU KV space into multiple grain sizes (tiny, small, medium, large) tuned from observed allocation histograms. Allocation picks the smallest grain class that fits the request to avoid oversized reservations.
- Maintain compacted "anchor slots" for long-lived contexts (can be pinned by model+user key) so their allocations are immune to micro-shuffles and preferentially compacted around them.
- Background micro-healing worker that performs localized compaction: identifies adjacent free micro-slabs and coalesces while respecting real-time latency SLOs using off-peak or low-util windows.
- Hybrid eviction metric: combine recency (LRU-like), step-affinity (same generation hotness), and write-amplification estimate (cost to reload) to avoid evicting entries whose reload cost would spike tail latency.
- Allocation hinting exposed to the request router: short-lived requests (e.g., single-turn completions) can request a transient allocation class enabling fast reclaim without compaction.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Full defragmentation vs localized healing: Full defrag is intrusive and would cause jitter; we choose targeted local coalesce to keep stable tail latencies.
- Granularity of tessellation: More classes reduce internal fragmentation but increase management overhead; we target 4 classes initially and allow dynamic tuning via telemetry.
- Anchors add complexity and can cause space reservation; anchors are only allowed with explicit pin hints (via rollout-controlled API) and have quotas per model/instance.

Telemetry and metrics to drive tuning:
- Allocation-size histogram (per-model, per-region) with percentiles and heatmap over time windows.
- Fragmentation index: free-gaps-weighted-by-size / total-allocatable to quickly surface micro-hole regressions.
- Reclamation churn: counts of micro-healing operations, bytes moved, and reclaimed.
- Eviction cost estimator: observed reload latency for rehydrated entries and tokens regenerated.
- Continuous-batching co-occurrence matrix: co-located allocation lifetimes when batching N>1 to measure cross-request interference.

Implementation plan (phased):
1) Instrumentation (2 wks): Add allocation histograms and simple fragmentation index telemetry to production sampling. No allocator change.
2) Tessellation allocator prototype (3 wks): In-memory, runtime-flag gated. Implement tiny/small/medium/large classes with first-fit within class and per-class free lists. Unit + performance tests in staging.
3) Anchor API and quotas (1 wk): Add pin hint metadata, enforce per-model quotas and rate-limited anchor admission.
4) Micro-healing worker (2 wks): Background compaction that moves small allocations into contiguous slots with move operations gated by latency budget checks.
5) Hybrid eviction policy (2 wks): Replace current LRU-only policy with recency+affinity+reload-cost. Add feature flag for rollout.
6) Canary rollout + measurement (2 wks): Progressive rollout on a small subset of Dedicated pools, monitor fragmentation index, p50/p95/p99 latency, and token cost.

Acceptance criteria:
- Fragmentation index improves by >=35% on sampled mixed-length workloads in staging after enabling tessellation + healing.
- p99 generation latency does not regress by more than 5% under comparable load during canary.
- Eviction-induced reload token cost reduced by >=20% on test traces representing conversational workloads.
- No increase in critical GPU OOMs in canary clusters; micro-healing performed within configured latency budget.

Testing and validation:
- Synthetic allocator stress tests reproducing mixed-length lifetime distributions, continuous batching with batch sizes 1-8, and pinned anchor churn.
- Replay real production traces in a dedicated test harness to compute expected reload cost improvements.
- Fuzzing of anchor admission quotas and healing worker interrupts to ensure safety.

Rollout plan:
- Feature-flagged across runtime; enable metrics-only for 1 week, then enable tessellation allocator in read-only simulated mode (accounting only), then enable live on 3 Dedicated pools with heavy-metrics baseline, then increase to 20% of traffic, 50%, then global if metrics pass.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: micro-healing moves could spike memory bandwidth and hurt tail latency. Mitigation: rate-limit move throughput, prioritize idle GPU cycles and respect latency headroom hooks from scheduler.
- Risk: anchors lead to unseen reservation storms. Mitigation: strict quotas, automated anchor eviction heuristics if pressure spikes.
- Risk: mis-tuned grain sizes increase internal fragmentation. Mitigation: ship with telemetry + remote-configbed grain thresholds and automatic adjustment experiments.

Open engineering questions:
- Should the return path include a fast-path for cross-batch copy avoidance (zero-copy when same batch allocation reuse)?
- How to best attribute reload cost to multi-tenant scenarios for eviction decisions?
- Exact thresholds for anchor admission under pressure and tie-breakers for eviction vs compaction.

Related artifacts:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood/example/kv-tessellation (draft)
- Perf harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/kv-perf-playground/pulls/154
- Telemetry dashboard: https://grafana.redwood/example/kv-frag-dashboard

Next steps:
- Owner (Asha) to kick off instrumentation spike and gather 72-hour production samples.
- Schedule design walkthrough with Runtime and Scheduler teams week of 2026-03-15.

implementation_plan: Phase 1: telemetry only (2w). Phase 2: tessellation allocator behind flag (3w). Phase 3: anchors + quotas (1w). Phase 4: micro-healing worker (2w). Phase 5: hybrid eviction (2w). Phase 6: canary + progressive rollout (2w).
telemetry: Allocation-size histograms, fragmentation index, reclamation churn, eviction reload cost, continuous-batching co-occurrence matrix. Dashboards and alert thresholds to be added to runtime team Grafana. Sampling for 1% production requests initially.
